newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul's OECD entry to shake up financial sector.
newsitem.headline: Seoul's OECD entry to shake up financial sector.

text.p: South Korea is bracing for a wave of mergers and acquisitions among banks and brokerages following entry to the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), analysts said on Monday.
But they noted restructuring would come slowly, citing difficulties in cutting jobs.

"Banks and brokerage houses have to prepare for rapid market liberalisation through mergers and acquisitions," said Kim Byong-sok, a financial analyst at Hannuri-Salomon Securities. "The trend will be to get bigger."
South Korea was invited on Friday to join the Paris-based club of rich nations.
Since applying for OECD membership in March 1995, South Korea has speeded up liberalisation of its financial markets to foreign investors and pledged further reforms.
"Joining the OECD will be good news in the long term for the financial sector," said Kim.
Banks are seen as most vulnerable to foreign competition after being sheltered in the past, and they are likely to be most affected by the shakeup, analysts said.
Foreign banks will be permitted to set up wholly-owned subsidiaries in South Korea by the end of 1998.
"The government wants to promote mergers between large commercial banks that would enable them to compete against foreign banks," said Lee Seung-hoon, a financial analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

"The ideal would be for a big city bank to merge with a regional bank. The city bank would have a strong metropolitan presence and the regional bank would have a strong regional presence and there would be less overlapping."
The South Korean government will play a strong role in restructuring. It plans to encourage mergers and acquisitions partly through tax incentives.
But difficulties in laying off employees are expected to slow down restructuring.

"The concept is culturally rather difficult to accept," said Kim Min-tae, a reseach fellow at the LG Economic Research Institute. South Korean labour law makes it virtually impossible to lay off staff.
Analysts said the importance of cutting jobs to improve efficiency would be a hard message to get across to the public.
"For a successful merger or acquisition, cost efficiency is the key," Kim said. "You can't have efficiency unless you've cut jobs. But there is no legal ground in South Korea to lay off people."
Deregulation of the financial industry will ultimately strengthen banks, who have been hobbled by government-directed lending to large corporations, analysts said.
"The underlying profitability of banks will rise along with government deregulation," said Lee of Morgan Grenfell.
"Freed from restrictions, banks can engage more in profit-oriented activities and have better control over credit screening," he said.
